We now pass from one generator to finitely many.

**Lemma 4.1 (Downward Closure of the Family Certificate).** For every finite witness family $W$, the generated family $\mathcal C(W)$ is downward closed.

**Proof sketch.** If $s\in\mathcal C(W)$, then $s\subseteq w$ for some $w\in W$. For any $t\subseteq s$, transitivity gives $t\subseteq w$, so $t\in\mathcal P(w)\subseteq\mathcal C(W)$. $\square$

**Lemma 4.2 (Witness Retention).** Every requested witness is retained:

$$
W\subseteq\mathcal C(W).
$$

**Proof sketch.** For each $w\in W$, reflexivity gives $w\in\mathcal P(w)$, and this principal certificate is one of the families in the defining union. $\square$

**Theorem 4.3 (Family Certificate Minimality).** Let $K$ be downward closed and suppose $W\subseteq K$. Then

$$
\mathcal C(W)\subseteq K.
$$

Consequently, $\mathcal C(W)$ is the unique least downward-closed family containing $W$.

**Proof sketch.** Fix $w\in W$. Since $w\in K$, Theorem 3.3 gives $\mathcal P(w)\subseteq K$. Taking the union over all $w\in W$ gives $\mathcal C(W)\subseteq K$. Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 show that $\mathcal C(W)$ itself satisfies the required conditions. $\square$

This theorem justifies defining the intrinsic witness complexity of $W$ by

$$
\kappa(W)=|\mathcal C(W)|.
$$

It is not the size of a chosen construction among many; it is the minimum cardinality of any downward-closed family retaining all witnesses. Indeed, every admissible family contains the generated certificate.

Several elementary structural properties follow immediately.

**Proposition 4.4 (Monotonicity).** If $W_1\subseteq W_2$, then

$$
\mathcal C(W_1)\subseteq\mathcal C(W_2)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\kappa(W_1)\le\kappa(W_2).
$$

**Proof sketch.** Every principal certificate occurring in the first union also occurs in the second. $\square$

**Proposition 4.5 (Idempotence).** Applying downward generation twice has no effect:

$$
\mathcal C(\mathcal C(W))=\mathcal C(W).
$$

**Proof sketch.** The family $\mathcal C(W)$ is already downward closed, so every subset generated from one of its faces remains inside it. Conversely, each face belongs to its own principal certificate. $\square$

**Proposition 4.6 (Redundant Generator Elimination).** If $u,v\in W$ and $u\subseteq v$, then removing $u$ from $W$ does not change the generated certificate, provided $v$ remains.

**Proof sketch.** Inclusion $u\subseteq v$ implies $\mathcal P(u)\subseteq\mathcal P(v)$. Hence the term contributed by $u$ is already covered by that contributed by $v$. $\square$

Repeatedly applying Proposition 4.6 reduces $W$ to its inclusion-maximal members, which form an antichain. This compression is exact rather than approximate.

## 5. The two-parameter theorem

We now derive the principal quantitative estimate.

**Theorem 5.1 (Two-Parameter Witness Bound).** Let $W$ be a finite witness family. Suppose

$$
|W|\le q
$$

and

$$
|w|\le m\quad\text{for every }w\in W.
$$

Then $\mathcal C(W)$ is downward closed, contains $W$, and satisfies

$$
|\mathcal C(W)|\le q2^m.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Downward closure and witness retention are Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2. For cardinality, the union bound and Theorem 3.4 give

$$
|\mathcal C(W)|
=\left|\bigcup_{w\in W}\mathcal P(w)\right|
\le\sum_{w\in W}|\mathcal P(w)|
=\sum_{w\in W}2^{|w|}.
$$

Since $|w|\le m$, monotonicity of exponentiation gives $2^{|w|}\le2^m$. Therefore

$$
|\mathcal C(W)|
\le |W|2^m
\le q2^m.
$$

$\square$

**Corollary 5.2 (Existence of a Small Witness Subcomplex).** Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.1, there exists a finite downward-closed family $K$ such that

$$
W\subseteq K
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|K|\le q2^m.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Take $K=\mathcal C(W)$. $\square$

The statement is independent of the cardinality of the ambient vertex set $V$. Vertices not used by the witnesses play no role. In fact, the vertex support of $\mathcal C(W)$ is contained in $\bigcup_{w\in W}w$, whose cardinality is at most $qm$, though overlap may make it much smaller.

The roles of $q$ and $m$ are qualitatively different. At fixed width, adding witnesses contributes at most linearly. At fixed number of witnesses, increasing width by one can double the bound. The one-witness lower bound proves that this exponential dependence on width is unavoidable in general.

## 6. Compatibility with an ambient complex

The intrinsic construction remains internal to any ambient complex containing the witnesses.

**Theorem 6.1 (Ambient Subcomplex Theorem).** Let $A$ be a finite downward-closed family and let $W\subseteq A$. If $|W|\le q$ and $|w|\le m$ for all $w\in W$, then there exists a finite family $K$ satisfying

$$
K\text{ is downward closed},
$$

$$
W\subseteq K\subseteq A,
$$

and

$$
|K|\le q2^m.
$$

The least such family under inclusion is $K=\mathcal C(W)$.

**Proof sketch.** Choose $K=\mathcal C(W)$. Theorem 5.1 gives downward closure, witness retention, and the cardinality bound. Since $A$ is downward closed and contains $W$, Theorem 4.3 gives $\mathcal C(W)\subseteq A$. Minimality among all downward-closed families containing $W$ is also Theorem 4.3. $\square$

The theorem separates construction from environment. The ambient complex may contain many vertices and faces, but only the designated witnesses and their subsets are required. Nevertheless, the certificate is not external: it is a true subcomplex of $A$.

## 7. Overlap-sensitive enumeration

The estimate $q2^m$ ignores overlap among principal certificates. Exact counting follows from a useful identity.

**Lemma 7.1 (Intersection of Principal Certificates).** For finite faces $u$ and $v$,

$$
\mathcal P(u)\cap\mathcal P(v)=\mathcal P(u\cap v).
$$

More generally, for nonempty finite $I\subseteq W$,

$$
\bigcap_{w\in I}\mathcal P(w)=\mathcal P\left(\bigcap_{w\in I}w\right).
$$

**Proof sketch.** A face lies in every $\mathcal P(w)$ exactly when it is a subset of every $w$, which is equivalent to being a subset of their intersection. $\square$

**Corollary 7.2 (Exact Two-Witness Formula).** For finite faces $u$ and $v$,

$$
|\mathcal C(\{u,v\})|
=2^{|u|}+2^{|v|}-2^{|u\cap v|}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Apply the two-set inclusion–exclusion formula, Theorem 3.4, and Lemma 7.1. $\square$

**Theorem 7.3 (Exact Inclusion–Exclusion Formula).** Let $W$ be nonempty. Then

$$
|\mathcal C(W)|
=
\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq W}
(-1)^{|I|+1}
2^{\left|\bigcap_{w\in I}w\right|}.
$$

**Proof sketch.** Apply finite inclusion–exclusion to the family of sets $\{\mathcal P(w):w\in W\}$. Lemma 7.1 identifies each intersection as a principal certificate, and Theorem 3.4 counts it. $\square$

This formula is exact but involves up to $2^{|W|}-1$ terms. It is therefore best viewed as a structural description or an algorithm for small $q$. Pairwise or higher-order intersection data can support cheaper bounds.

The universal bound is generally strict. If $W$ contains $q$ nonempty, pairwise disjoint faces of width $m$, their principal certificates intersect exactly in the empty face. Their union has

$$
1+q(2^m-1)=q2^m-(q-1)
$$

faces, already below $q2^m$. Equality in the naive union bound requires pairwise disjoint principal certificates, which is impossible for two nonempty witness families because both contain the empty face. Thus $q2^m$ is a convenient uniform ceiling, not normally an attainable exact value when $q>1$.

## 8. Algorithms

### 8.1 Direct certificate generation

Represent each face in canonical form, such as a sorted tuple or immutable set. For each witness, enumerate every subset and insert it into a hash set.

**Algorithm 8.1 (Principal-Union Certificate Construction).**

**Input:** A finite witness family $W$.  
**Output:** The least downward-closed family $\mathcal C(W)$ containing $W$.

1. Initialize an empty set $K$.
2. For each witness $w\in W$:
   1. Fix an ordering $w=(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$.
   2. For each bit mask $b$ from $0$ to $2^r-1$:
      1. Form $s_b=\{v_i:\text{bit }i\text{ of }b\text{ is }1\}$.
      2. Insert $s_b$ into $K$.
3. Return $K$.

**Correctness sketch.** The inner loop enumerates $\mathcal P(w)$ exactly. The outer loop takes the union over $w\in W$, so the output is $\mathcal C(W)$. Theorems 4.1–4.3 establish downward closure, retention, and minimality. $\square$

If $|W|\le q$ and every witness has width at most $m$, there are at most $q2^m$ generated subsets before deduplication. Constructing each subset naively costs $O(m)$, giving time $O(qm2^m)$ and output storage $O(q2^m)$ faces, with representation-dependent factors.

### 8.2 Maximal-antichain compression

Before generating subsets, remove every witness properly contained in another witness.

**Algorithm 8.2 (Maximal Witness Compression).**

1. Initialize $M=W$.
2. For each ordered pair of distinct witnesses $(u,v)$:
   1. If $u\subseteq v$, delete $u$ from $M$.
3. Return $M$.

**Correctness sketch.** Proposition 4.6 shows that each deletion preserves the generated certificate. After all deletions, $M$ consists exactly of inclusion-maximal witnesses and $\mathcal C(M)=\mathcal C(W)$. $\square$

With straightforward set comparisons, the preprocessing uses $O(q^2m)$ time and $O(qm)$ input storage. It can greatly reduce the effective value of $q$ when witnesses are nested.

### 8.3 Inclusion–exclusion counting

When only the cardinality is needed and $q$ is small, one may avoid materializing all faces.

**Algorithm 8.3 (Intersection-Profile Counting).**

1. Set an integer accumulator $T=0$.
2. For every nonempty subfamily $I\subseteq W$:
   1. Compute $r_I=|\bigcap_{w\in I}w|$.
   2. Add $(-1)^{|I|+1}2^{r_I}$ to $T$.
3. Return $T$.

**Correctness sketch.** This is exactly Theorem 7.3. $\square$

A direct implementation takes $O(2^qqm)$ time in a simple representation and uses little space beyond the input. Incremental intersection updates can reduce constants. This algorithm is complementary to direct generation: it is exponential in the number of witnesses rather than in witness width.

## 9. A false global extrapolation

It is important not to confuse generated-certificate complexity with the total size of an arbitrary bounded-width complex.

**Proposition 9.1 (Width Two Does Not Imply $2n$ Faces).** There exists a downward-closed complex on four vertices, all of whose faces have size at most two, with eleven faces. In particular, its number of faces is not $2n$, since $11\ne8$ for $n=4$.

**Proof sketch.** Let the vertex set have four elements and include every subset of cardinality at most two. The family is downward closed. It has one empty face, four vertices, and $\binom42=6$ edges, hence

$$
1+4+6=11.
$$

$\square$

The formula $2n$ does hold for the clique complex of a tree on $n$ vertices: there are one empty face, $n$ vertices, and $n-1$ edges. But this uses the tree’s edge count. Width two by itself allows as many as $\binom n2$ edges, producing

$$
1+n+\binom n2
$$

faces in the complete width-two complex. The witness theorem remains valid because it includes the number $q$ of designated generators as a separate parameter.

## 10. Applications and interpretations

### 10.1 Local explanations in hereditary systems

Suppose a conclusion is supported by $q$ feature interactions, each involving at most $m$ features, and the explanatory language requires all subinteractions to be included. The generated explanation then has at most $q2^m$ components. The total vocabulary size is irrelevant. This favors sparse, narrow witnesses and makes explicit that reducing width can be more consequential than reducing ambient dimension.

### 10.2 Geometric witness selection

Carathéodory-type arguments seek a simplex whose convex hull contains a target point. Once a witness simplex with at most $d+1$ vertices is selected, its least simplicial certificate has exactly

$$
2^{d+1}
$$

faces when all $d+1$ vertices are used. The selection theorem supplies the witness; the principal certificate theorem supplies the exact hereditary package. In colorful variants, a rainbow simplex can therefore be retained inside the colorful join with a certificate controlled by dimension rather than by the total number of input points.

### 10.3 Topological data analysis

Large filtered complexes often contain localized features represented by selected simplices or cycles supported on a small set of maximal faces. Retaining the selected maximal faces forces their downward closures. The family certificate gives a canonical preprocessing target and a transparent worst-case size. Overlap-sensitive counting quantifies savings when selected simplices share boundaries.

### 10.4 Databases and configuration systems

If feasible configurations are hereditary under deletion of choices, then a requested configuration forces every subconfiguration. A family of configurations generates precisely the union of their power sets. The same theory measures the smallest hereditary subdatabase preserving the designated records.

### 10.5 Independence complexes

For a matroid, independent sets form a downward-closed family. A selected basis of rank $r$ forces all $2^r$ of its subsets within the independence complex. Several selected bases yield a certificate bounded by $q2^r$, with potentially substantial savings determined by basis intersections. Matroid exchange structure may permit sharper bounds than arbitrary set systems.

## 11. Discussion

The principal certificate has three properties that rarely coincide so cleanly: it is canonical, minimal under inclusion, and exactly countable. Their combination makes witness complexity an intrinsic invariant rather than an artifact of a construction.

The two-parameter estimate is strongest in regimes where the ambient system is huge but explanations are local. It should not be read as a claim that every bounded-dimensional complex is small. The counterexample in Section 9 demonstrates that the multiplicity of maximal faces must be controlled. Parameters $q$ and $m$ capture precisely that distinction.

There are two natural notions of optimality. For one witness, $2^{|w|}$ is exactly optimal and forced. For several witnesses, $\mathcal C(W)$ is exactly optimal as a family, but the coarse numerical estimate $q2^m$ need not equal its cardinality. The discrepancy contains meaningful information about overlap. In this sense, minimality settles the optimization problem, while enumeration remains a combinatorial problem governed by intersections.

The exact inclusion–exclusion formula suggests a dual algorithmic landscape. Direct generation is fixed-parameter tractable in width $m$ when $q$ is moderate and the output is required. Inclusion–exclusion counting is suitable when $q$ is small even if individual witnesses are wide. Hybrid methods may exploit both parameters, repeated intersection patterns, or a compressed maximal antichain.

## 12. Future directions

First, overlap-sensitive inequalities should interpolate between the universal union bound and exact inclusion–exclusion. Bounds expressed through pairwise intersection widths may provide useful estimates without enumerating all subfamilies.

Second, maximal-antichain compression deserves a quantitative theory. Since non-maximal generators are redundant, complexity should be parameterized by the size, width, and intersection profile of the maximal antichain.

Third, one may characterize extremal families maximizing $|\mathcal C(W)|$ for fixed $q$, $m$, and perhaps a fixed ambient support size. Because every principal certificate shares the empty face, the value $q2^m$ is generally unattainable for multiple nonempty witnesses; the correct sharp extremal expression should account for mandatory overlap.

Fourth, the combinatorial result can be coupled directly to colorful Carathéodory selection. A rainbow simplex in dimension $d$ has at most $d+1$ vertices and therefore admits an exact principal certificate of at most $2^{d+1}$ faces inside the colorful join.

Finally, analogous witness theories can be developed for closure systems beyond simplicial complexes. Independence complexes retain downward closure, while greedoids, convex geometries, and other accessible systems modify it. Identifying the correct principal object and its cardinality in each setting would extend intrinsic witness complexity beyond the Boolean lattice.

## 13. Conclusion

A finite face $w$ does not stand alone in a downward-closed world: it brings every subset with it. This forced shadow is exactly its power set, has $2^{|w|}$ faces, and is the least valid certificate. A family $W$ generates the union of these shadows, again the unique least certificate. Consequently, at most $q$ witnesses of width at most $m$ can always be retained in a downward-closed family of at most $q2^m$ faces, independently of ambient size and without leaving an ambient complex that already contains them.

The result gives a precise local principle: hereditary certificates are governed by the number and width of the witnesses, while their overlap determines the savings beyond the universal bound.

\begin{abstract}
We study the size of a finite downward-closed family required to retain a prescribed collection of finite witness sets. For a witness $w$, its principal certificate is its power set $\Pow(w)$. We prove that this is the unique least downward-closed family containing $w$, has exactly $2^{|w|}$ members, and gives both an attainable upper bound and a universal lower bound for one-witness complexity. For a family $W$, the generated certificate is $\Cert(W)=\bigcup_{w\in W}\Pow(w)$. It is the unique least downward-closed family containing $W$. If $W$ has at most $q$ members and every member has cardinality at most $m$, then $|\Cert(W)|\le q2^m$, independently of the number of ambient vertices. If $W$ lies in an ambient downward-closed family $A$, then $\Cert(W)\subseteq A$. We also give exact overlap formulas, construction and compression algorithms, and a counterexample showing that bounded face width alone does not imply an analogous global face count.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Many existence arguments produce a small \emph{witness}: a finite set or face certifying a target property. In a hereditary combinatorial structure, retaining that witness requires retaining all of its subobjects. For an abstract simplicial complex, every subset of a face must itself be a face. Certificate size is therefore the size of the downward-closed family generated by the designated witnesses.

Let $W$ be a finite family of finite sets. Two intrinsic parameters are
\[
q\ge |W|,\qquad m\ge \max_{w\in W}|w|.
\]
The central estimate is
\[
|\Cert(W)|\le q2^m,
\]
where $\Cert(W)$ is the union of the power sets of all witnesses. This improves ambient-size estimates whenever $q$ and $m$ are small. It separates multiplicity, which contributes linearly, from width, which contributes exponentially. For one witness the exponential is exact.

The bound is universal but generally not numerically sharp for several witnesses, because principal certificates overlap. Their exact cardinality is governed by intersections. A crucial scope distinction is that the theorem bounds the subcomplex generated by designated witnesses; width alone does not bound an arbitrary complex by $2n$. The complete width-two complex on four vertices has eleven faces rather than eight.

\section{Definitions}
Let $V$ be an arbitrary vertex set. Every face below is a finite subset of $V$, and every family of faces is finite.

\begin{definition}[Downward-closed family]
A family $K$ is \emph{downward closed} if $s\in K$ and $t\subseteq s$ imply $t\in K$. A finite abstract simplicial complex is precisely such a family.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Witness and width]
A \emph{witness} is a designated finite face $w\subseteq V$, with width $|w|$. A witness family is a finite family $W$ of witnesses. Its width is $\max_{w\in W}|w|$ when nonempty, and may be taken as zero when empty.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Principal and family certificates]
The principal certificate generated by $w$ is
\[
\Pow(w)=\{s\subseteq V:s\subseteq w\}.
\]
The family certificate generated by $W$ is
\[
\Cert(W)=\bigcup_{w\in W}\Pow(w)
=\{s\subseteq V:\text{some }w\in W\text{ satisfies }s\subseteq w\}.
\]
\end{definition}

Thus $\Cert(W)$ is the order ideal generated by $W$ in the finite-subset poset.

\section{Exact one-witness complexity}
\begin{lemma}[Principal downward closure]
For every finite witness $w$, the family $\Pow(w)$ is downward closed and contains $w$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $s\subseteq w$ and $t\subseteq s$, transitivity gives $t\subseteq w$. Moreover, $w\subseteq w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Principal Certificate Minimality]
If $K$ is downward closed and $w\in K$, then
\[
\Pow(w)\subseteq K.
\]
Consequently, $\Pow(w)$ is the unique least downward-closed family containing $w$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every $s\in\Pow(w)$ satisfies $s\subseteq w$. Downward closure of $K$ therefore forces $s\in K$. The preceding lemma shows that $\Pow(w)$ is itself admissible, and a least family under inclusion is unique.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Principal Complexity]
For every finite witness $w$,
\[
|\Pow(w)|=2^{|w|}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each element of $w$, a subset independently chooses inclusion or exclusion. Equivalently, subsets are in bijection with functions $w\to\{0,1\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Universal One-Witness Lower Bound]
If $K$ is downward closed and $w\in K$, then
\[
2^{|w|}\le |K|.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Minimality gives $\Pow(w)\subseteq K$; apply monotonicity of cardinality and the exact count.
\end{proof}

Thus the cost $2^{|w|}$ is not an artifact of an estimate: it is forced by hereditary closure.

\section{Families of witnesses}
\begin{lemma}[Closure and retention]
For every finite witness family $W$, the family $\Cert(W)$ is downward closed and $W\subseteq\Cert(W)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $s\in\Cert(W)$, then $s\subseteq w$ for some $w\in W$. Any $t\subseteq s$ also satisfies $t\subseteq w$. Each $w$ belongs to its own power set, proving retention.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Family Certificate Minimality]
If $K$ is downward closed and $W\subseteq K$, then
\[
\Cert(W)\subseteq K.
\]
Consequently, $\Cert(W)$ is the unique least downward-closed family containing $W$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For every $w\in W$, principal minimality gives $\Pow(w)\subseteq K$. Taking the union over $W$ proves the inclusion. Closure and retention show admissibility.
\end{proof}

It is therefore natural to define intrinsic witness complexity by
\[
\kappa(W)=|\Cert(W)|.
\]
This is the minimum cardinality of any downward-closed family retaining $W$.

\begin{proposition}[Monotonicity, idempotence, and redundancy]
The generated certificate has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item If $W_1\subseteq W_2$, then $\Cert(W_1)\subseteq\Cert(W_2)$.
\item $\Cert(\Cert(W))=\Cert(W)$.
\item If $u,v\in W$ and $u\subseteq v$, deleting $u$ while retaining $v$ does not change $\Cert(W)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Part (i) follows by comparing the defining unions. For (ii), $\Cert(W)$ is already downward closed and contains each of its own members. For (iii), $u\subseteq v$ implies $\Pow(u)\subseteq\Pow(v)$, so the term generated by $u$ is redundant.
\end{proof}

Repeated redundancy elimination reduces $W$ to its inclusion-maximal members, an antichain, without changing the certificate.

\section{The intrinsic two-parameter bound}
\begin{theorem}[Two-Parameter Witness Theorem]
Let $W$ be a finite witness family with $|W|\le q$ and $|w|\le m$ for every $w\in W$. Then $\Cert(W)$ is downward closed, contains $W$, and
\[
|\Cert(W)|\le q2^m.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Closure and retention were proved above. By the union bound and the exact principal count,
\[
|\Cert(W)|
\le \sum_{w\in W}|\Pow(w)|
=\sum_{w\in W}2^{|w|}
\le |W|2^m
\le q2^m.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Small Witness Subcomplex]
Under the theorem's hypotheses, there exists a downward-closed family $K$ with $W\subseteq K$ and $|K|\le q2^m$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Take $K=\Cert(W)$.
\end{proof}

The estimate contains no ambient vertex count. The support of the certificate is contained in $\bigcup_{w\in W}w$, of size at most $qm$, but even this support estimate is not required for the face bound.

\section{Compatibility with an ambient complex}
\begin{theorem}[Ambient Subcomplex Theorem]
Let $A$ be a finite downward-closed family and $W\subseteq A$. If $|W|\le q$ and $|w|\le m$ for every $w\in W$, then there is a downward-closed $K$ such that
\[
W\subseteq K\subseteq A,
\qquad |K|\le q2^m.
\]
The least such family under inclusion is $K=\Cert(W)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The two-parameter theorem supplies closure, retention, and the size bound for $K=\Cert(W)$. Since $A$ is downward closed and contains $W$, family minimality gives $\Cert(W)\subseteq A$.
\end{proof}

Thus the bound forgets ambient scale without disconnecting the certificate from its environment.

\section{Overlap-sensitive enumeration}
\begin{lemma}[Intersections of principal certificates]
For finite faces $u,v$,
\[
\Pow(u)\cap\Pow(v)=\Pow(u\cap v).
\]
More generally, for every nonempty finite subfamily $I$,
\[
\bigcap_{w\in I}\Pow(w)=\Pow\left(\bigcap_{w\in I}w\right).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A face belongs to every principal certificate exactly when it is a subset of every generator, equivalently a subset of their intersection.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Two-witness formula]
For finite faces $u,v$,
\[
|\Cert(\{u,v\})|=2^{|u|}+2^{|v|}-2^{|u\cap v|}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the two-set inclusion--exclusion identity, the intersection lemma, and the principal count.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Inclusion--Exclusion Formula]
For every nonempty finite witness family $W$,
\[
|\Cert(W)|=
\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq W}
(-1)^{|I|+1}2^{\left|\bigcap_{w\in I}w\right|}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply finite inclusion--exclusion to $\{\Pow(w):w\in W\}$. The intersection lemma identifies every intersection, and exact principal complexity counts it.
\end{proof}

The general estimate is normally strict. If $q$ nonempty width-$m$ witnesses are pairwise disjoint, their principal certificates share exactly the empty face, and the union has
\[
1+q(2^m-1)=q2^m-(q-1)
\]
faces. Intersection structure measures the savings beyond the universal ceiling.

\section{Algorithms}
\begin{algorithm}[Principal-Union Certificate Construction]
Given $W$, initialize an empty set $K$. For each $w\in W$, order its vertices as $v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1}$. For each bit mask from $0$ through $2^r-1$, form the subset containing $v_i$ exactly when bit $i$ is one, and insert it into $K$. Return $K$.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{proposition}[Correctness and complexity]
The principal-union algorithm returns $\Cert(W)$, hence the unique least downward-closed certificate containing $W$. If $|W|\le q$ and widths are at most $m$, its naive running time is $O(qm2^m)$ and its output contains at most $q2^m$ faces.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The inner loop enumerates $\Pow(w)$ exactly, and the outer loop unions these families. There are at most $q2^m$ generated subsets, each requiring $O(m)$ work in a direct representation.
\end{proof}

\begin{algorithm}[Maximal-Antichain Compression]
Compare pairs of witnesses and delete any witness properly contained in another retained witness. Return the inclusion-maximal witnesses.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{proposition}[Compression correctness]
Maximal-antichain compression preserves $\Cert(W)$. A straightforward implementation takes $O(q^2m)$ time for witnesses of width at most $m$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every deletion is justified by the redundancy proposition. At most quadratically many pairs are compared, each in $O(m)$ time in a suitable set representation.
\end{proof}

\begin{algorithm}[Intersection-Profile Counting]
Initialize $T=0$. For every nonempty subfamily $I\subseteq W$, compute $r_I=|\bigcap_{w\in I}w|$ and add $(-1)^{|I|+1}2^{r_I}$ to $T$. Return $T$.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{proposition}[Counting correctness]
Intersection-profile counting returns $|\Cert(W)|$. A direct implementation takes $O(2^q q m)$ time and need not materialize the certificate.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Correctness is the exact inclusion--exclusion theorem. The stated cost bounds the computation of an intersection for each of $2^q-1$ nonempty subfamilies.
\end{proof}

\section{A false global extrapolation}
\begin{proposition}[Width two does not imply $2n$ faces]
There is a downward-closed complex on four vertices, all of whose faces have size at most two, with eleven faces. Thus its face count is not $2n$, since $11\ne8$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Include every subset of four vertices having cardinality at most two. This is downward closed and contains one empty face, four singleton faces, and $\binom42=6$ edges. Its cardinality is
\[
1+4+6=11.
\]
\end{proof}

A tree on $n$ vertices does have $2n$ faces in its clique complex: one empty face, $n$ vertices, and $n-1$ edges. The equality comes from tree sparsity, not width two. The complete width-two complex has $1+n+\binom n2$ faces. This distinction explains why the witness count $q$ is indispensable.

\section{Applications}
\subsection{Hereditary explanations}
If a conclusion is supported by at most $q$ feature interactions, each involving at most $m$ features, and explanations must include all subinteractions, the least hereditary explanation has at most $q2^m$ components. The vocabulary outside those interactions is irrelevant. Width reduction can therefore be more valuable than ambient-dimension reduction.

\subsection{Geometric selection}
Carath\'eodory-type arguments select a simplex whose convex hull contains a target. A simplex on at most $d+1$ vertices has a principal certificate of at most $2^{d+1}$ faces, exactly $2^{d+1}$ when it uses all $d+1$ vertices. In colorful variants, selection of a rainbow simplex can therefore be followed by an ambient-independent certificate inside the colorful join.

\subsection{Topological data and configurations}
A selected simplex in a large complex forces its boundary faces. Several selected maximal simplices generate precisely their family certificate, with overlap savings when they share boundaries. The same structure appears in hereditary databases: a retained configuration forces all subconfigurations.

\subsection{Independence complexes}
Independent sets of a matroid form a downward-closed family. A selected basis of rank $r$ forces all $2^r$ subsets; $q$ selected bases generate at most $q2^r$ independent sets. Basis intersections and exchange structure may yield stronger bounds than those available for arbitrary set systems.

\section{Discussion and future work}
The principal certificate is canonical, inclusion-minimal, and exactly countable. These properties turn witness complexity into an intrinsic invariant. For one witness, both the optimal family and its size are known exactly. For many witnesses, the optimal family remains exact, but its cardinality reflects overlap and can be substantially below $q2^m$.

Several directions follow. First, pairwise and higher-order intersection bounds should interpolate between the union bound and full inclusion--exclusion. Second, antichain compression suggests parameterizing complexity by the number and width of maximal generators. Third, one can seek sharp extremal formulas for fixed $q$ and $m$; mandatory sharing of the empty face already prevents the naive upper bound from usually being attained for multiple nonempty witnesses. Fourth, colorful Carath\'eodory selection can be combined with the certificate theorem so that one rainbow simplex yields an exact $2^{d+1}$-face package. Finally, independence complexes invite matroidal refinements governed jointly by rank, selected bases, and their intersection pattern.

\section{Conclusion}
A face in a downward-closed world brings every subset with it. Its forced shadow is its power set, with exactly $2^{|w|}$ faces, and this is the least valid certificate. A family of witnesses generates the union of these shadows, again the unique least certificate. Hence at most $q$ witnesses of width at most $m$ can be retained in a downward-closed subcomplex of at most $q2^m$ faces, independently of ambient size and without leaving any ambient complex that already contains them. The number and width of witnesses determine the universal cost; their overlap determines the savings.

from itertools import combinations
from math import comb
from typing import FrozenSet, Iterable, Iterator, Sequence, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
Face = FrozenSet[T]
Complex = set[Face[T]]


def powerset(face: Face[T]) -> Iterator[Face[T]]:
    """Yield every subset of ``face`` exactly once."""
    items = tuple(face)
    for size in range(len(items) + 1):
        for subset in combinations(items, size):
            yield frozenset(subset)


def principal_certificate(face: Face[T]) -> Complex[T]:
    """Return the least downward-closed family containing one face."""
    return set(powerset(face))


def family_certificate(witnesses: Iterable[Face[T]]) -> Complex[T]:
    """Return the union of the principal certificates of all witnesses."""
    certificate: Complex[T] = set()
    for witness in witnesses:
        certificate.update(powerset(witness))
    return certificate


def maximal_witnesses(witnesses: Iterable[Face[T]]) -> set[Face[T]]:
    """Delete witnesses contained in another witness without changing closure."""
    family = set(witnesses)
    return {w for w in family if not any(w < other for other in family)}


def is_downward_closed(family: set[Face[T]]) -> bool:
    """Check the hereditary closure condition by explicit subset enumeration."""
    return all(subset in family for face in family for subset in powerset(face))


def two_parameter_bound(witnesses: Sequence[Face[T]]) -> int:
    """Compute q * 2^m using the actual witness count and maximum width."""
    q = len(witnesses)
    m = max((len(w) for w in witnesses), default=0)
    return q * (2**m)


def inclusion_exclusion_count(witnesses: Sequence[Face[T]]) -> int:
    """Count the family certificate from all nonempty witness intersections."""
    total = 0
    q = len(witnesses)
    for size in range(1, q + 1):
        sign = 1 if size % 2 == 1 else -1
        for chosen in combinations(witnesses, size):
            intersection = set(chosen[0])
            for witness in chosen[1:]:
                intersection.intersection_update(witness)
            total += sign * (2 ** len(intersection))
    return total


def format_face(face: Face[object]) -> str:
    """Format a face deterministically for display."""
    return "{" + ", ".join(map(str, sorted(face, key=str))) + "}"


def demonstrate_single_witness() -> None:
    """Show exact 2^|w| complexity and the forced lower bound."""
    witness: Face[int] = frozenset({1, 2, 3, 4, 5})
    certificate = principal_certificate(witness)
    expected = 2 ** len(witness)
    assert len(certificate) == expected
    assert is_downward_closed(certificate)
    print("1. Exact principal-certificate complexity")
    print(f"   witness width: {len(witness)}")
    print(f"   certificate faces: {len(certificate)} = 2^{len(witness)}")
    histogram = {r: sum(len(face) == r for face in certificate)

    print(f"   faces by dimension level: {histogram}")
    print(f"   binomial prediction: {[comb(len(witness), r) for r in range(6)]}\n")

    """Compare the universal bound with exact overlap-sensitive complexity."""
    witnesses: list[Face[int]] = [

    print("2. Overlap savings and maximal-antichain compression")
    print(f"   input witnesses: {len(witnesses)}; maximal witnesses: {len(compressed)}")

    vertices = frozenset({1, 2, 3, 4})

    expected = 1 + n + comb(n, 2)

    assert count == expected == 11
    assert count != 2 * n
    print("3. Width-two counterexample to a global 2n formula")
    print(f"   vertices: {n}")
    print(f"   faces: 1 + {n} + C({n},2) = {count}")
    print(f"   proposed 2n value: {2*n}")
    print("   conclusion: width alone does not control total face count.\n")


def demonstrate_ambient_independence() -> None:
    """Show that unused ambient vertices do not change a certificate."""
    witnesses: list[Face[int]] = [
        frozenset({10, 20, 30}),
        frozenset({30, 40}),

    print(f"   designated witnesses: {len(witnesses)}")
    print(f"   generated certificate faces: {len(small)}")
    print(f"   intrinsic upper bound: {two_parameter_bound(witnesses)}")


def main() -> None:
    """Run all numerical demonstrations."""
    print("INTRINSIC WITNESS COMPLEXITY — NUMERICAL DEMONSTRATIONS\n")
    demonstrate_single_witness()
    demonstrate_overlap_and_compression()
    demonstrate_width_two_counterexample()
    demonstrate_ambient_independence()

## Results established

The intrinsic two-parameter theorem replaces an ambient-vertex polynomial estimate by a bound determined by the witnesses themselves. For a finite family $W$ of designated faces, let its generated certificate be the union of all power sets of members of $W$. If $W$ has at most $q$ members and every member has at most $m$ vertices, then the generated certificate is downward closed, contains every designated face, and has at most $q2^m$ faces. This bound is independent of the number of ambient vertices. If $W$ lies in an ambient downward-closed complex, the certificate lies in that complex as well.

For a single face $w$, its power set is the least downward-closed certificate containing $w$, and its size is exactly $2^{|w|}$. Thus the exponential dependence on witness width is exact for one witness, rather than an artifact of the upper-bound proof.

## Contrarian conjecture tested

A tempting extrapolation from tree clique complexes is that every width-two complex on $n$ vertices might have exactly $2n$ faces. This is false: the complete width-two skeleton on four vertices has eleven faces, whereas $2n=8$.

## Strong next questions

1. **Overlap-sensitive bounds.** Replace $q2^m$ by an exact inclusion–exclusion formula, or bounds in terms of pairwise intersection sizes of maximal witness faces.
2. **Antichain compression.** Show systematically that deleting non-maximal members of $W$ leaves its generated certificate unchanged, then bound complexity via the width and size of the maximal antichain.
3. **Sharp extremal family theorem.** Characterize when the generated certificate comes closest to $q2^m$; disjoint $m$-faces still share the empty face, so the displayed general estimate is usually not attained.
4. **Geometric bridge.** Combine arbitrary-dimensional colorful Carathéodory selection with the intrinsic certificate theorem so that one rainbow simplex yields an exact $2^{d+1}$-face certificate inside the colorful join.
5. **Matroidal witnesses.** Replace simplicial downward closure by independence complexes and seek bounds governed jointly by rank and the number of selected bases.",

    witnesses: list[Face[int]] = [
        frozenset({1, 2, 3, 4}),
        frozenset({3, 4, 5, 6}),
        frozenset({1, 2}),  # redundant: contained in the first witness
    ]
    compressed = maximal_witnesses(witnesses)
    certificate = family_certificate(witnesses)
    compressed_certificate = family_certificate(compressed)
    bound = two_parameter_bound(witnesses)
    exact_ie = inclusion_exclusion_count(witnesses)
    assert certificate == compressed_certificate
    assert exact_ie == len(certificate)
    assert len(certificate) <= bound
    assert is_downward_closed(certificate)
    print("2. Overlap savings and maximal-antichain compression")
    print(f"   input witnesses: {len(witnesses)}; maximal witnesses: {len(compressed)}")
    print(f"   universal q*2^m bound: {bound}")
    print(f"   exact generated size: {len(certificate)}")
    print(f"   inclusion-exclusion count: {exact_ie}")
    print(f"   saved faces versus bound: {bound - len(certificate)}\n")


def demonstrate_width_two_counterexample() -> None:
    """Construct the complete width-two complex on four vertices."""
    vertices = frozenset({1, 2, 3, 4})
    complex_: Complex[int] = {
        face for face in powerset(vertices) if len(face) <= 2
    }
    n = len(vertices)
    count = len(complex_)
    expected = 1 + n + comb(n, 2)
    assert is_downward_closed(complex_)
    assert count == expected == 11
    assert count != 2 * n
    print("3. Width-two counterexample to a global 2n formula")
    print(f"   vertices: {n}")
    print(f"   faces: 1 + {n} + C({n},2) = {count}")
    print(f"   proposed 2n value: {2*n}")
    print("   conclusion: width alone does not control total face count.\n")


def demonstrate_ambient_independence() -> None:
    """Show that unused ambient vertices do not change a certificate."""
    witnesses: list[Face[int]] = [
        frozenset({10, 20, 30}),
        frozenset({30, 40}),
    ]
    small = family_certificate(witnesses)
    # Adding a million conceptual ambient labels changes no witness subset.
    ambient_vertex_count = 1_000_000
    same = family_certificate(witnesses)
    assert small == same
    print("4. Independence from ambient scale")
    print(f"   conceptual ambient vertices: {ambient_vertex_count:,}")
    print(f"   designated witnesses: {len(witnesses)}")
    print(f"   generated certificate faces: {len(small)}")
    print(f"   intrinsic upper bound: {two_parameter_bound(witnesses)}")


def main() -> None:
    """Run all numerical demonstrations."""
    print("INTRINSIC WITNESS COMPLEXITY — NUMERICAL DEMONSTRATIONS\n")
    demonstrate_single_witness()
    demonstrate_overlap_and_compression()
    demonstrate_width_two_counterexample()
    demonstrate_ambient_independence()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Future Directions: Sharp maximal excess of the ℤ₂ co-index under joins

This cycle established the constructive, lower-bound half of the co-index theory:
the join of free ℤ₂-complexes satisfies
`coind(K * L) ≥ coind(K) + coind(L) + 1`,
with the octahedral spheres forming a join-monoid `Oct m * Oct n ≅ Oct(m+n+1)`, and
the classical suspension jump recovered as the special case `L = S⁰`. The following
conjectures push toward the sharp equality and the full maximal-excess phenomenon.

## Conjecture 1 (Sharp join law)
For free ℤ₂-complexes `K, L`, the co-index is *exactly* additive with a shift:
`coind(K * L) = coind(K) + coind(L) + 1`.
The key insight is that the lower bound is realised by an explicit coordinate-split
equivariant map, so the entire difficulty concentrates in a single matching upper
bound `coind(K * L) ≤ coind(K) + coind(L) + 1`, which should follow from a
ℤ₂-index (equivariant cohomology) obstruction that is itself additive under joins.
Why now? The join bifunctor and its explicit connecting map are now in hand, so the
only missing ingredient is a purely obstruction-theoretic upper bound — a
self-contained, isolable target.

## Conjecture 2 (Maximal excess for all feasible starting co-index)
For all integers `d ≥ 2` and `c` with `1 ≤ c ≤ d`, there is a finite free
ℤ₂-complex `K` of dimension `d` with `coind(K) = c` and `coind(S K) = d + 1`.
The key insight is that the "excess" `d + 1 - c` can be manufactured by joining a
low-co-index but high-dimensional building block (a complex whose co-index is
pinned below its dimension by a Borsuk–Ulam obstruction) with a sphere that supplies
the missing co-index only after one further suspension. Why now? The join
construction gives a flexible dial for dimension independent of co-index, exactly
the freedom needed to separate `c` from `d`.

## Conjecture 3 (Borsuk–Ulam upper bound in the octahedral tower)
Any equivariant simplicial map `Oct n → Oct k` forces `n ≤ k`; equivalently
`coind(Oct k) = k` on the nose.
The key insight is that the base case (no equivariant map to `Oct 0` from a
higher sphere) already isolates the parity/degree obstruction, and the general case
should follow by an inductive "peel one coordinate" argument compatible with the
join splitting `Oct k ≅ Oct 0 * Oct(k-1)`. Why now? The join splitting turns the
global obstruction into a one-step induction that reuses the verified base case.

## Conjecture 4 (Excess is monotone but not superadditive under iterated suspension)
Writing `S^j K` for the `j`-fold suspension, the excess sequence
`e_j := coind(S^j K) - (dim(S^j K))` is non-increasing in `j` and stabilises at
`0` after finitely many steps.
The key insight is that each suspension can raise the co-index by *at most* one while
raising the dimension by exactly one, so the gap can only shrink; stabilisation at
`0` is the assertion that suspension eventually saturates the Borsuk–Ulam bound.
Why now? The exact `+1` dimension law and the `≥ +1` co-index law are both proved,
so the monotonicity direction is within reach and only the saturation needs the
upper bound of Conjecture 1.

import Applications.Z2CoindexJoinClassification

/-!
# Finite composition law for the ℤ₂ co-index

This development connects equivariant topology with the additive bookkeeping of finite composite
systems.  A `FiniteFreeSystem` is a nonempty finite free ℤ₂-system.  Its binary composition is the
simplicial join, and `composeMany` is the right-associated composition of an arbitrary finite list.

The principal result, `coind_composeMany`, proves the exact many-body law

`coind (K₀ ⋆ K₁ ⋆ ⋯ ⋆ Kᵣ) = ∑ᵢ coind Kᵢ + r`.

Thus the shifted quantity `coind K + 1` is extensive: it is exactly additive under composition.
This simultaneously extends the two-factor classification theorem from the catalog and the earlier
multi-join theorem, which was restricted to octahedral spheres.
-/

namespace Z2CoindexFiniteComposition

open Z2CoindexJoin

/-- A finite, nonempty free ℤ₂-system.  The chosen vertex records nonemptiness; no basepoint is
preserved by morphisms or used in the invariant. -/
structure FiniteFreeSystem where
  /-- The underlying free ℤ₂-set. -/
  space : FreeZ2
  /-- Finiteness of the vertex set. -/
  finiteV : Fintype space.V
  /-- A witness that the system is nonempty. -/
  vertex : space.V

attribute [instance] FiniteFreeSystem.finiteV

/-- Binary composition of finite free systems is their equivariant simplicial join. -/
def FiniteFreeSystem.compose (A B : FiniteFreeSystem) : FiniteFreeSystem where
  space := A.space ⋆ B.space
  finiteV := instFintypeJoinV A.space B.space
  vertex := Sum.inl A.vertex

/-- Right-associated composition of a head system with a list of further systems. -/
def composeMany : FiniteFreeSystem → List FiniteFreeSystem → FiniteFreeSystem
  | A, [] => A
  | A, B :: Bs => A.compose (composeMany B Bs)

/-- The list of co-indices of the tail systems. -/
noncomputable def tailCoindices (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) : List ℕ := As.map (fun A => Z2CoindexJoin.coind A.space)

/-- The number of vertices in a finite composite is the sum of the vertex counts of its factors.
-/
theorem card_composeMany (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    Fintype.card (composeMany A As).space.V =
      Fintype.card A.space.V + (As.map (fun B => Fintype.card B.space.V)).sum := by
  induction' As with B Bs ih generalizing A;
  · rfl;
  · convert congr_arg₂ ( · + · ) rfl ( ih B ) using 1;
    convert Fintype.card_sum

/-- **Exact finite composition law.**  For arbitrary finite nonempty free ℤ₂-systems, the co-index
of a right-associated join is the sum of the factor co-indices plus one for every join operation.
Unlike the octahedral multi-join law, no sphere hypothesis is imposed on any factor.
-/
theorem coind_composeMany (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    Z2CoindexJoin.coind (composeMany A As).space =
      Z2CoindexJoin.coind A.space + (tailCoindices As).sum + As.length := by
  revert A As;
  intro A As
  induction' As with B As ih generalizing A;
  · aesop;
  · convert coind_join_eq_general A.vertex ( composeMany B As ).vertex using 1;
    simp +arith +decide [ ih, tailCoindices ]

/-- The shifted co-index is extensive under an arbitrary finite composition: it converts joins into
ordinary addition.
-/
theorem shifted_coind_composeMany (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    Z2CoindexJoin.coind (composeMany A As).space + 1 =
      (Z2CoindexJoin.coind A.space + 1) + (As.map (fun B => Z2CoindexJoin.coind B.space + 1)).sum := by
  induction As <;> simp_all +decide [ add_assoc, List.sum_cons ];
  · rfl;
  · rename_i k hk ih; rw [ coind_composeMany ] ; simp +arith +decide [*] ;
    rfl

/-- Vertex counting and co-index extensivity agree exactly on every finite composite system.
-/
theorem two_mul_shifted_coind_eq_card (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    2 * (Z2CoindexJoin.coind (composeMany A As).space + 1) =

/-!
# Finite composition law for the ℤ₂ co-index

This development connects equivariant topology with the additive bookkeeping of finite composite
systems.  A `FiniteFreeSystem` is a nonempty finite free ℤ₂-system.  Its binary composition is the
simplicial join, and `composeMany` is the right-associated composition of an arbitrary finite list.

The principal result, `coind_composeMany`, proves the exact many-body law

`coind (K₀ ⋆ K₁ ⋆ ⋯ ⋆ Kᵣ) = ∑ᵢ coind Kᵢ + r`.

Thus the shifted quantity `coind K + 1` is extensive: it is exactly additive under composition.
This simultaneously extends the two-factor classification theorem from the catalog and the earlier
multi-join theorem, which was restricted to octahedral spheres.
-/

namespace Z2CoindexFiniteComposition

open Z2CoindexJoin

/-- A finite, nonempty free ℤ₂-system.  The chosen vertex records nonemptiness; no basepoint is
preserved by morphisms or used in the invariant. -/
structure FiniteFreeSystem where
  /-- The underlying free ℤ₂-set. -/
  space : FreeZ2
  /-- Finiteness of the vertex set. -/
  finiteV : Fintype space.V
  /-- A witness that the system is nonempty. -/
  vertex : space.V

attribute [instance] FiniteFreeSystem.finiteV

/-- Binary composition of finite free systems is their equivariant simplicial join. -/
def FiniteFreeSystem.compose (A B : FiniteFreeSystem) : FiniteFreeSystem where
  space := A.space ⋆ B.space
  finiteV := instFintypeJoinV A.space B.space
  vertex := Sum.inl A.vertex

/-- Right-associated composition of a head system with a list of further systems. -/
def composeMany : FiniteFreeSystem → List FiniteFreeSystem → FiniteFreeSystem
  | A, [] => A
  | A, B :: Bs => A.compose (composeMany B Bs)

/-- The list of co-indices of the tail systems. -/
noncomputable def tailCoindices (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) : List ℕ := As.map (fun A => Z2CoindexJoin.coind A.space)

/-- The number of vertices in a finite composite is the sum of the vertex counts of its factors.
-/
theorem card_composeMany (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    Fintype.card (composeMany A As).space.V =
      Fintype.card A.space.V + (As.map (fun B => Fintype.card B.space.V)).sum := by
  induction' As with B Bs ih generalizing A;
  · rfl;
  · convert congr_arg₂ ( · + · ) rfl ( ih B ) using 1;
    convert Fintype.card_sum

/-- **Exact finite composition law.**  For arbitrary finite nonempty free ℤ₂-systems, the co-index
of a right-associated join is the sum of the factor co-indices plus one for every join operation.
Unlike the octahedral multi-join law, no sphere hypothesis is imposed on any factor.
-/
theorem coind_composeMany (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    Z2CoindexJoin.coind (composeMany A As).space =
      Z2CoindexJoin.coind A.space + (tailCoindices As).sum + As.length := by
  revert A As;
  intro A As
  induction' As with B As ih generalizing A;
  · aesop;
  · convert coind_join_eq_general A.vertex ( composeMany B As ).vertex using 1;
    simp +arith +decide [ ih, tailCoindices ]

/-- The shifted co-index is extensive under an arbitrary finite composition: it converts joins into
ordinary addition.
-/
theorem shifted_coind_composeMany (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    Z2CoindexJoin.coind (composeMany A As).space + 1 =
      (Z2CoindexJoin.coind A.space + 1) + (As.map (fun B => Z2CoindexJoin.coind B.space + 1)).sum := by
  induction As <;> simp_all +decide [ add_assoc, List.sum_cons ];
  · rfl;
  · rename_i k hk ih; rw [ coind_composeMany ] ; simp +arith +decide [*] ;
    rfl

/-- Vertex counting and co-index extensivity agree exactly on every finite composite system.
-/
theorem two_mul_shifted_coind_eq_card (A : FiniteFreeSystem) (As : List FiniteFreeSystem) :
    2 * (Z2CoindexJoin.coind (composeMany A As).space + 1) =
      Fintype.card (composeMany A As).space.V := by
  exact Z2CoindexJoin.two_mul_coind_succ_eq_card (composeMany A As).vertex

import Mathlib.GroupTheory.Perm.Fin
import Novelty.FactorialCRTObstruction

/-!
# Equivariant factorial codes

A factorial code of length `k` chooses its digit at position `i` from
`Fin (i + 1)`.  The recursive presentation makes the mixed-radix structure
explicit.  The central equivalence identifies these codes with permutations of
`Fin k`; transporting left multiplication then equips the code space with a
free and transitive symmetric-group action.

The final result records a sharp boundary: this set-theoretic and equivariant
classification does not turn the digits into independent Chinese-remainder
coordinates.  At length four, the corresponding residue product is not even
additively equivalent to `ZMod (4!)`.
-/

namespace EquivariantFactorialCodes

/-- Mixed-radix factorial codes: digit `i` lies in `Fin (i + 1)`. -/
abbrev FactorialCode (k : Nat) := ∀ i : Fin k, Fin (i.val + 1)

/-- Splitting off the highest-radix digit is an equivalence. -/
def codeSuccEquiv (k : Nat) :
    FactorialCode (k + 1) ≃ Fin (k + 1) × FactorialCode k :=
  (Fin.snocEquiv (fun i : Fin (k + 1) => Fin (i.val + 1))).symm

/-- The recursive Lehmer classification, aligned with permutation
`decomposeFin` at every stage. -/
def permCodeEquiv : (k : Nat) → Equiv.Perm (Fin k) ≃ FactorialCode k
  | 0 => Equiv.ofUnique _ _
  | k + 1 =>
      Equiv.Perm.decomposeFin |>.trans
        ((Equiv.prodCongr (Equiv.refl _) (permCodeEquiv k)).trans
          (codeSuccEquiv k).symm)

/-- Encoding a permutation as its factorial code. -/
def encode {k : Nat} : Equiv.Perm (Fin k) → FactorialCode k := permCodeEquiv k

/-- Decoding a factorial code to the classified permutation. -/
def decode {k : Nat} : FactorialCode k → Equiv.Perm (Fin k) := (permCodeEquiv k).symm

@[simp] theorem decode_encode {k : Nat} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) :
    decode (encode σ) = σ := by
  exact (permCodeEquiv k).symm_apply_apply σ

@[simp] theorem encode_decode {k : Nat} (c : FactorialCode k) :
    encode (decode c) = c := by
  exact (permCodeEquiv k).apply_symm_apply c

# Future Directions: Seidel energy of Turán graphs under edge deletion

This cycle established the elementary spectral-moment foundations of Seidel
energy: the Seidel matrix is real symmetric with vanishing first moment
`tr S = 0` and a *graph-independent* second moment `tr S² = n(n-1)`, from which a
universal energy floor `E_S ≥ √(n(n-1))` follows by Cauchy–Schwarz, and the
Seidel spectrum is invariant under switching. The most instructive finding is a
negative one: the second moment is completely blind to edge deletion, which
explains why the Turán edge-deletion inequality is genuinely delicate. The
following conjectures build on that structural insight.

## Conjecture 1 (Strict edge-deletion inequality on Turán graphs)
For every Turán graph `T(n, r)` with `r ≥ 4` and `n ≥ 4r`, and every edge `e`,
the Seidel energy strictly increases upon deletion: `E_S(T(n,r) − e) > E_S(T(n,r))`.

*The key insight is* that although the first two spectral moments are identical
for `T(n,r)` and `T(n,r) − e`, deleting an edge flips two symmetric Seidel entries
from `−1` to `+1`, a rank-two, trace-zero perturbation whose effect on the energy
is governed entirely by how it redistributes eigenvalue mass across zero — a
higher-moment quantity the sphere constraint cannot see.

*Why now?* The reduced-order description of Turán (blow-up) Seidel spectra has
matured to the point where the perturbation can be tracked on a low-dimensional
quotient, making a fully rigorous account of the two flipped entries feasible.

## Conjecture 2 (Energy is a strict switching-refinement monotone)
Within a fixed switching class, Seidel energy is minimised exactly at the
conference-type representatives, and strictly increases as the spectrum spreads
away from the two-point mass on `±√(n-1)`.

*The key insight is* that the fixed second moment confines every spectrum in a
switching class to a common sphere, so energy — the ℓ¹ norm of the eigenvalues —
is maximised by spreading and minimised by concentration, turning energy
comparison into a majorization statement on the sphere `∑λ² = n(n-1)`.

*Why now?* Switching invariance of the whole spectrum (established here at the
eigenpair level) lets one compare energies across an entire class by a single
majorization argument rather than case-by-case eigenvalue computation.

## Conjecture 3 (Rank-two perturbation formula for edge flips)
Flipping a single Seidel entry pair changes the characteristic polynomial by an
explicit degree-`(n−2)` correction, and the resulting energy change has a fixed
sign determined by the number of eigenvalues the flip pushes across `0`.

*The key insight is* that an edge flip is a symmetric rank-two update
`S ↦ S + 2(e_a e_bᵀ + e_b e_aᵀ)`, so the matrix determinant lemma yields the new
characteristic polynomial in closed form, reducing the energy change to a
counting problem about sign changes of eigenvalues.

*Why now?* Closed-form rank-two spectral updates are standard, but they have not
been combined with the fixed-second-moment constraint of Seidel matrices; doing
so converts an analytic energy inequality into an eigenvalue-counting identity.

## Conjecture 4 (Universal floor is asymptotically sharp only for conference graphs)
The universal bound `E_S ≥ √(n(n-1))` is attained asymptotically (ratio → 1) if
and only if the graph is a conference two-graph, and every other family is bounded
away from the floor by a constant factor.

*The key insight is* that equality in the Cauchy–Schwarz step forces all
eigenvalues to have equal magnitude, which for a trace-zero `±1` off-diagonal
matrix on the sphere `∑λ² = n(n-1)` is exactly the conference (regular two-graph)
condition.

*Why now?* Regular two-graphs and conference matrices are now catalogued far
enough (via their equivalence with certain strongly regular graphs) to test the
"only if" direction against all known sporadic families.

/-!
# Factorial codes classify finite permutations

A length-`k` factorial code has digit `i` in `Fin (i+1)`.  This file proves
that these codes classify permutations of `Fin k`.  The construction factors
through numerical factoradic rank: the value of a code is the weighted sum
`∑ i, cᵢ i!`, and the recursive permutation rank uses the standard
`decomposeFin` equivalence.

namespace FactorialLehmerClassification

open Equiv Finset

/-- The factorial-code space of length `k`. -/
abbrev FactorialCode (k : Nat) := ∀ i : Fin k, Fin (i.val + 1)

/-- Evaluation of a factorial code. -/
def codeValue {k : Nat} (c : FactorialCode k) : Nat :=
  ∑ i : Fin k, (c i).val * i.val.factorial

/-
Factorial evaluation always lies in `[0,k!)`.
-/
theorem codeValue_lt {k : Nat} (c : FactorialCode k) :
    codeValue c < k.factorial := by
  induction' k with k ih <;> simp_all +decide [ Fin.sum_univ_castSucc, codeValue ];
  rw [ Nat.factorial_succ, mul_comm ];
  nlinarith! [ ih ( fun i => c i.castSucc ), Fin.is_lt ( c ( Fin.last k ) ) ]

/-
Factorial evaluation is injective on bounded codes.
-/
theorem codeValue_injective {k : Nat} {c d : FactorialCode k}
    (h : codeValue c = codeValue d) : c = d := by
  induction' k with k ih;
  · exact Subsingleton.elim _ _;
  · -- By definition of `codeValue`, we can write
    have h_split : codeValue c = c (Fin.last k) * Nat.factorial k + codeValue (fun i => c i.castSucc) ∧ codeValue d = d (Fin.last k) * Nat.factorial k + codeValue (fun i => d i.castSucc) := by
      unfold codeValue; simp +decide [ Fin.sum_univ_castSucc ] ;
      exact ⟨ add_comm _ _, add_comm _ _ ⟩;
    -- By the properties of factorial codes, we know that $c (Fin.last k) = d (Fin.last k)$.
    have h_last : c (Fin.last k) = d (Fin.last k) := by
      have h_last : codeValue (fun i => c i.castSucc) < Nat.factorial k ∧ codeValue (fun i => d i.castSucc) < Nat.factorial k := by
        exact ⟨ codeValue_lt _, codeValue_lt _ ⟩;
      exact Fin.ext ( by nlinarith );
    ext i; induction i using Fin.lastCases <;> simp_all +decide ;
    exact congr_arg Fin.val ( congr_fun ( ih h ) _ )

/-
There are exactly `k!` factorial codes of length `k`.
-/
theorem card_factorialCode (k : Nat) :
    Fintype.card (FactorialCode k) = k.factorial := by
  induction' k with k ih <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.factorial_succ ];
  rw [ ← ih, Fin.prod_univ_castSucc ] ; norm_num;
  ring

/-- Factorial evaluation, regarded as a map into `Fin (k!)`. -/
def codeRank (k : Nat) (c : FactorialCode k) : Fin k.factorial :=
  ⟨codeValue c, codeValue_lt c⟩

/-- Evaluation gives the complete numerical classification of factorial codes. -/
noncomputable def codeRankEquiv (k : Nat) : FactorialCode k ≃ Fin k.factorial :=
  Equiv.ofBijective (codeRank k) <|

      intro c d h

def rankPermEquiv : (k : Nat) → Fin k.factorial ≃ Equiv.Perm (Fin k)
  | 0 => (finCongr (by simp : Nat.factorial 0 = 1)).trans (Equiv.ofUnique _ _)
  | k + 1 =>

        finProdFinEquiv.symm.trans <|
          (Equiv.prodCongr (Equiv.refl (Fin (k + 1))) (rankPermEquiv k)).trans <|
            Equiv.Perm.decomposeFin.symm

/-- The canonical Lehmer classification induced by factoradic evaluation and
recursive decomposition of finite permutations. -/
noncomputable def lehmerEquiv (k : Nat) :
    FactorialCode k ≃ Equiv.Perm (Fin k) :=
  (codeRankEquiv k).trans (rankPermEquiv k)

The permutation rank of a factorial code is exactly its factoradic
numerical evaluation.
-/
theorem lehmer_rank_eq_codeValue (k : Nat) (c : FactorialCode k) :
    ((rankPermEquiv k).symm (lehmerEquiv k c)).val = codeValue c := by
  unfold lehmerEquiv; aesop;

Every permutation has a unique factorial code.
-/
theorem existsUnique_code (k : Nat) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k)) :
    ∃! c : FactorialCode k, lehmerEquiv k c = σ := by

## Small cases

The number of length-`k` codes is the product of digit radices `1·2···k = k!`.

| `k` | code radices | number of codes | number of permutations |
|---:|:---|---:|---:|
| 0 | empty | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1,2 | 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 1,2,3 | 6 | 6 |
| 4 | 1,2,3,4 | 24 | 24 |
| 5 | 1,2,3,4,5 | 120 | 120 |

These six code counts are certified by `small_card_counts` in
`Catalog/Pythagorean/FactorialLehmerClassification.lean`; the general equality
is `card_factorialCode`.

For `k = 3`, the evaluations are exactly `0,1,2,3,4,5`: the digits have bounds
`c₀=0`, `c₁∈{0,1}`, `c₂∈{0,1,2}`, and value `c₁ + 2c₂`.

## Sequence identification

The counts `1, 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ...` are the factorial numbers, OEIS A000142.

## Counterexample hunt

No small counterexample occurs for `k = 0,...,5`. More strongly, the Lean proof
is universal: `codeValue_lt` bounds every code value, `codeValue_injective`
proves distinct codes have distinct values, and `card_factorialCode` proves the
domain and `[0,k!)` have equal finite cardinality. The equivalence
`lehmerEquiv` then classifies every permutation for every natural `k`.
